text: Every device needs an IP address, a subnet mask, a default gateway, and a DNS server before it can do anything useful on a network. Configuring all of that by hand on every laptop and phone doesn't scale. DHCP automates the whole handoff — a device joins the network, asks, and gets fully configured within a second or two, with no human involved.

The process is four steps, known as DORA. Discover: the device broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER, asking if any DHCP server is out there. Offer: a server replies with a proposed address and configuration. Request: the device broadcasts back which offer it's accepting. Acknowledge: the server confirms, and the device can start using that address immediately.

All four messages are broadcasts, even though the server is really replying to one specific device. The client has no IP address yet, so it has no way to send a normal unicast packet, and every DHCP server on the segment needs to see the request so a server whose offer wasn't chosen knows to let that address go.

A DHCP offer is a full bundle, not just an address: subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers, and a lease time — how long that configuration is valid. Around the halfway point of the lease, the device quietly renews directly with the server, usually keeping the same address with no visible interruption at all.

DHCP isn't used for everything, though. A server, a printer, or a router's own management interface is usually given a static IP instead, configured once by hand, so other devices can always find it at the same fixed address, instead of one that might change after every reboot.
